overview: The United States declared independence from Britain in 1776, won recognition after war and established its present constitutional framework in the late 1780s. Its history is also the history of Indigenous nations, enslaved and free Black people, immigrants and many other communities whose experiences differed sharply. Expansion brought invention and opportunity for some, while others faced removal, forced labor or exclusion. Schools, kitchens, washrooms, workplaces and protests show how people lived and changed the country. The United States continues as a state.

periods.title: Independence and a federal constitution
periods.summary: Thirteen colonies declared independence in 1776 and later won recognition. Delegates signed a federal Constitution in 1787; ratification and a new government followed. Revolutionary ideals did not reach all residents equally.

periods.title: Expansion, exclusion and competing freedoms
periods.summary: The new federal system gained a Bill of Rights. Westward expansion depended on Indigenous dispossession, including forced removal, while slavery continued and spread in the growing country.

periods.title: Civil War, emancipation and Reconstruction
periods.summary: The Civil War ended with the defeat of the Confederacy. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in 1865, but Black communities had to fight for citizenship, schooling, safety and political power during and after Reconstruction.

periods.title: Industry, migration and overseas power
periods.summary: Factories and immigration reshaped cities, while Jim Crow denied many Black Americans equal rights. The 1898 war with Spain brought overseas territories under U.S. control, with different local political futures.

periods.title: Votes, depression and world war
periods.summary: Women won a constitutional guarantee against denial of voting rights on account of sex in 1920. After the 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, the United States entered World War II; its government also imprisoned Japanese Americans without evidence of individual wrongdoing.

periods.title: Civil rights and a Moon landing
periods.summary: Organized civil rights action helped secure legal changes in schooling, public accommodations and voting. Public health improved through clean water and vaccines. In 1969 Apollo 11 landed humans on the Moon.

periods.title: A continuing, changing society
periods.summary: The state and its communities continue beyond any single map snapshot. A 1983 child's lunch box is one small object from this later period; it cannot summarize the whole country, but it reminds us that history includes ordinary mornings as well as national events.

sections.title: Founding and the gap between words and lives

items.text: On 4 July 1776, representatives of thirteen colonies issued a Declaration of Independence. Recognition and the new government took more time. The famous claim of equality was a political ideal that excluded many people in practice, including enslaved people and women.

Delegates signed a Constitution in Philadelphia in 1787. The first ten amendments, called the Bill of Rights, were ratified in 1791 after debate over the new federal government. Rights and their enforcement have been argued over and changed ever since.

The United States expanded across lands where Indigenous nations already governed, farmed, traded and raised families. From about 1830 to 1850, federal policy used treaties, fraud, intimidation and violence to remove roughly 100,000 Native people west of the Mississippi. Their nations and descendants continue.

Most Cherokee opposed the 1835 Treaty of New Echota signed by a small faction. Federal troops forced the main removal beginning in 1838. The Trail of Tears was an act of government power and tremendous human loss, not a voluntary family move.

The 1898 peace treaty after war with Spain transferred the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam to U.S. control while Spain relinquished Cuba. These places did not share one path afterward. A map of U.S. power must not make their residents invisible.

sections.title: Work, freedom and who could vote

items.text: The Thirteenth Amendment formally abolished slavery in 1865, after a war fought in part over its future. Formerly enslaved people organized conventions, schools and political campaigns. Black Codes and later Jim Crow laws tried to restrict that freedom.

In late nineteenth-century garment sweatshops, immigrant workers and sometimes families made clothes in crowded, unhealthy conditions. Some built better lives through this work; others endured illness and exhaustion. A finished coat could hide many hours of hands-on labor.

At Ellis Island, inspectors questioned arriving immigrants face to face and checked passenger lists. The interview could affect a family's future; U.S. immigration rules also excluded people in named categories. Ellis Island was one entry point, not the journey of every newcomer.

The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, barred denying a vote because of sex after decades of organizing. That did not remove racial barriers faced by many women or guarantee everyone practical access to the polls.

The 1965 Voting Rights Act attacked literacy tests and other devices used to keep Black citizens from voting, especially in the South. Organizers had faced threats and violence. The law marks a major change, not the end of every argument over voting.

American women wrote and used changing cookbooks in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. A recipe could carry a family taste, but printed books tell us more about literate cooks with access to ingredients than about every kitchen in the country.

At Virginia's Groveton one-room school, about 30 pupils learned different grades together, played baseball and kick-the-can at recess, and held spelling contests. Some boys missed class to help on farms. It is one school, not a nationwide timetable.

Schooling could be sharply unequal. In the same Virginia county, Black children often traveled farther to school than white children. Early twentieth-century Black communities and supporters built Rosenwald schools in the segregated South to improve opportunities that public systems denied.

A steel lunch box made in 1983 showed Disney characters going to school, fishing and playing marbles. It is a funny little reminder that children carried stories with their lunch. The object tells us about one commercial product, not what every child ate.

Working-class families in nineteenth-century tenements often lacked the running water available to wealthier households. Ideas about bathing changed over time, but a new soap advertisement could not install a faucet.

Archaeologists found three old privies, or outhouses, in early twentieth-century Seward, Alaska. A privy was a very practical place, but discarded objects in its pit can also help tell who lived nearby. This is a Seward example, not the design of every American toilet.

During the twentieth century, cleaner water systems cut diseases spread by contaminated water, and vaccines controlled several dangerous infections. These were public-health achievements built by many workers and communities, with access varying by place and time.

After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, the United States entered World War II. In 1942 the U.S. government forced about 122,000 Japanese Americans from West Coast homes into guarded camps. War did not make that mass incarceration just; the government later apologized and paid partial restitution.

Civil rights organizers challenged segregated schools, buses, lunch counters and voting barriers. Brown v. Board of Education and the 1964 Civil Rights Act were milestones, but people in local communities made change through organizing and risk.

Apollo 11 landed two humans on the Moon in July 1969 and brought all three crew members home. Astronauts Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins are famous, but the mission also required engineers, technicians and many others on Earth. It was a shared technical achievement, not just three people in a rocket.

sections.title: A short sample of written English

items.text: The 1776 Declaration includes the words “We hold these truths to be self-evident”. This is a short sample of English as transcribed by the National Archives from the Stone engraving; it is not a claim that English was the only language spoken or written in the new country.

The Declaration said people were equal while slavery continued and Indigenous lands were seized. Reading the words beside the lives they did not protect is one way to see why later generations kept demanding that the promise apply to them too.

ending.text: The United States continues; it has no historical collapse date to place at the end of this card. Its constitutional system and borders changed after 1776, and Indigenous nations, families and other communities have their own continuing histories within and across those borders. The imported map begins at 1783, after independence was declared, and its later snapshots show changing coverage rather than a final end.

sources.title: National Archives, Declaration of Independence: A Transcription
sources.note: July 4, 1776 Declaration; National Archives transcription notes it reflects the Stone engraving and original spelling; the 1776 language of equality existed alongside exclusions.

sources.title: National Archives, The Constitution: How Did it Happen?
sources.note: 1787 Philadelphia convention, September signature, slavery compromise, ratification and government framework; constitution did not grant equal rights to all residents.

sources.title: National Archives, Congress and the Bill of Rights in History and Today
sources.note: First ten constitutional amendments ratified in 1791; result of Federalist and Anti-Federalist debate over rights and central power.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, American Indian Removal
sources.note: Treaties, fraud, intimidation and violence removed roughly 100,000 American Indians from 1830 to 1850; created with tribal consultation, including Cherokee Nation.

sources.title: National Park Service, Trail of Tears History and Culture
sources.note: 1830 Removal Act, Cherokee majority opposed New Echota treaty and forced 1838 removal; specific nations and survival, not disappearance.

sources.title: National Museum of African American History and Culture, Defining Freedom
sources.note: Slavery, 1865 Thirteenth Amendment, Reconstruction, Black Codes, 1866 civil rights law, Jim Crow and long Black political struggle.

sources.title: National Park Service, Groveton School House
sources.note: Local Virginia one-room school with about 30 pupils; farm-season absences, recess games, and racial inequality in travel distance and schooling; local example only.

sources.title: National Park Service, The Rosenwald Schools
sources.note: Black communities and allies built improved schools in segregated South during early twentieth century; local initiative amid unequal public funding.

sources.title: Smithsonian Food History, Cooking Up History: Chicken Croquettes
sources.note: Smithsonian food-history handout: American women documented changing recipes in late eighteenth and nineteenth-century cookbooks; recipes represent literate cooks and particular households.

sources.title: National Museum of American History, History of Sweatshops 1880-1940
sources.note: Immigrant garment work in tenements, hazardous conditions, family labor and varied outcomes; specific industrial sector and period.

sources.title: National Park Service, Immigrant Inspector at Ellis Island
sources.note: Ellis Island inspection involved face-to-face questions, passenger manifests and exclusion criteria; not all immigrants entered through Ellis Island.

sources.title: National Park Service, The Seward Privy Project
sources.note: Excavated three early Seward, Alaska outhouses circa 1905-1920; archaeological privies can preserve discarded everyday objects, a local case.

sources.title: National Museum of American History, Bathing and Body Soaps
sources.note: Bathing habits, nineteenth-century promotion of bathing and unequal access to running water in working-class tenements.

sources.title: CDC, Ten Great Public Health Achievements: United States 1900-1999
sources.note: Twentieth-century water sanitation, vaccination and other public-health gains, with reductions in waterborne disease; population-level history, not universal access.

sources.title: National Archives, Nineteenth Amendment
sources.note: Ratified August 18, 1920 and barred denial of vote on account of sex; hard-won suffrage, with other barriers continuing.

sources.title: National Archives, Guide to House Records: Treaty of Paris 1898
sources.note: Treaty following Spanish-American War: Spain ceded Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam to United States and relinquished Cuba; imperial expansion with distinct later statuses.

sources.title: National Archives, Joint Address to Congress Leading to War with Japan
sources.note: December 7, 1941 Pearl Harbor attack and December 8 US declaration of war, entry into World War II.

sources.title: National Archives, Executive Order 9066
sources.note: 1942 order led to forced removal and incarceration of about 122,000 Japanese Americans, including citizens; 1988 official apology and partial restitution.

sources.title: National Park Service, The Story of Brown
sources.note: School desegregation struggle and civil rights movement; Brown v. Board and later protests, with 1964 Civil Rights Act milestone.

sources.title: National Archives, Voting Rights Act 1965
sources.note: August 6, 1965 act targeted literacy tests and other discriminatory voting barriers; based on civil rights organizing and Selma violence.

sources.title: NASA, Apollo 11
sources.note: 1969 Apollo 11 crewed lunar landing and return; Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins; national effort involved many workers beyond astronauts.

sources.title: National Museum of American History, School Days Lunch Box
sources.note: Specific 1983 Aladdin steel lunch box decorated with Disney school scenes; object reflects commercial childhood culture, not all lunches or families.
